title: UK to fight Russian disinformation and push new global AI standards, Burnham says
description: The UK will set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of hostile state attacks, including Russian disinformation, and lead efforts to establish
body: The UK will set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of hostile state attacks, including Russian disinformation, and lead efforts to establish global safety standards for artificial intelligence, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said.In his first major international speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, Burnham warned Russian agencies are using "every means at their disposal", including bots and fake websites, to "spread lies and disinformation". The prime minister noted AI will "multiply" existing threats, and pitched the UK as an "honest broker" on the technology.Fears about AI have grown after industry insiders recently warned it could threaten humanity.In Burnham's speech, he accused Russia of running a disinformation campaign."The Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion each year on manipulating information," Burnham told the UN General Assembly."They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC."We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair. "On top of that we have seen cyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. And we know that AI will multiply the threat."'He also referenced the 2019 UK general election, in which the government previously said Russia almost certainly sought to interfere.To counter this, Burnham announced a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt AI-enabled disinformation campaigns by hostile states.The centre will work alongside intelligence agencies, government departments, law enforcement and social media to bring together expertise to combat "information warfare".There was no immediate comment from Russia, a representative of which was sitting in the room listening to Burnham. When the UK government put out a report in 2020 about Russian activity in the UK, including in elections, Moscow described the allegations as "Russophobia".Addressing a forum about disinformation in Moscow on Tuesday, before the prime minister's speech, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Western media of embracing "anti-Russian cliches and fantasies".Before becoming prime minister, Burnham had said relatively little about how AI should be regulated.Since taking power in July, Burnham's government has stressed the need for international cooperation to combat the risks, as well as harness the potential benefits of the technology, warning that further regulation and legislation may be needed.In his speech, Burnham described the most advanced "Frontier AI" as "one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age".He told world leaders AI would be "key to economic growth" but also a "multiplier of risk".The prime minister added: "We've all heard the warnings – which we must heed. I know how worried people are. So we have to rise to this moment."Burnham said the "UK has a unique position as an honest broker", with close ties to the US and the European Union.He also highlighted the UK's "world-leading" AI Security Institute,  which was established under Conservative Prime Minister Rishi Sunak and tests major AI models to improve their safety before they are released publicly.He pledged to put AI "at the heart of the UK's G20 Presidency next year", when leaders of the world's biggest economies will gather in Manchester.Burnham said the UK would work towards agreeing a set of global principles and standards to ensure transparency, access to AI models, and that development happens safely.He added that this would "bring together welcome initiatives from others", such as a proposal from Norway this week.The declaration - which has the support of more than 20 countries, including Germany, Canada and Ireland - calls for AI to remain under human control and for mandatory pre-release testing of frontier models.However, it has not been signed by the US and China, which dominate AI development, or the UK.Former cabinet minister Darren Jones, who served as chief secretary to Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, called on the prime minister to sign the declaration and offer to broker an agreement with the US on its implementation.He argued there "should be a landing zone to agree mandatory testing", without undermining competitive advantage between companies and nations.The UK AI Security Institute's testing of AI models is currently on a voluntary basis and AI company Anthropic reportedly refused to submit its latest model for testing.Downing Street said officials had made clear in recent discussions with AI leaders that the government expects "full and total visibility of model developments".The prime minister has acknowledged that while developers have made significant commitments on transparency, nothing is off the table to keep the public safe, including legislation.Meanwhile, the government has announced a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.The Liberal Democrats and the Green Party have been putting pressure on the government to take further action on AI safety.However, any international efforts to regulate AI would need the cooperation of the US and China.In his own address earlier, US President Donald Trump rejected "any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI.Trump has dismissed warnings of AI destroying humanity as "a hoax" and rejected the idea of a global scheme to control the technology."We're going to encourage it, not rein it in," he told the UN General Assembly.Earlier in the day, Burnham and Trump had met, although Downing Street's statement on the meeting did not mention that they discussed AI.

schema.headline: UK to fight Russian disinformation and push new global AI standards, Burnham says

title: Lib Dems leave conference buoyed by Davey's message
description: This was a more sombre, more serious, Sir Ed Davey.The stunts - from falling off paddleboards to hurtling down rollercoasters – were scaled back at th
body: This was a more sombre, more serious, Sir Ed Davey.The stunts - from falling off paddleboards to hurtling down rollercoasters – were scaled back at this year's Liberal Democrat party conference."This is the fight of our lives," he repeatedly told his party. The focus, much like his conference speech last year, was on Reform UK.But the announcement he'd held back for his speech was aimed at Conservative-leaning voters: tax cuts worth billions.And not just for lower income earners, but for those in the higher 40% rate of tax too.Part of the announcement – raising the amount you can earn before you pay income tax altogether – was the same policy Davey's bête noire, Reform UK, announced at their conference a couple of weeks ago.The dividing line he drew was over how it was paid for. Nigel Farage's party would reduce spending on benefits to fund the tax cut. The Lib Dem leader said he would pay for it through the economic growth he believes could be gained by rejoining the EU's Single Market and a customs union.By putting the European Union at the heart of how he would fund his tax cut, the Lib Dems couldn't be drawing a starker contrast with the Brexit-backing Reform UK and a Conservative Party also committed to cutting welfare.But the plan is speculative. The Lib Dems insist a deal with the EU could be negotiated within a year if the party was in government after the next election.Plenty of economic experts, including the official budget forecaster the OBR, believe the UK's economy could grow if the UK was in the Single Market.But as recent political history teaches us, negotiating a deal with the European Union is often more difficult than party leaders hope. And basing a tax cut on potential future economic growth is a risky business.There is also uncertainty over whether the Lib Dems' sums add up. The independent  think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the policy as set out in the press release would cost "much more" than the £17bn the Lib Dems have budgeted for.The party says the tax cut wouldn't come in until the fifth year after the next election. So even if the party got into power and successfully negotiated an EU deal, the tax cut could be eight years away.But the Lib Dem MPs I spoke to afterwards were less focused on these details than the message it sent to voters.Davey came into this conference facing criticism over his leadership from some MPs in private and others in his party in public worrying about the party's ambition and direction.For now those concerns have been dampened. "That was the speech a lot of us have been waiting for him to give," one Davey-sceptic MP told me afterwards.A small number are uncomfortable with the main policy from the party's conference being a tax cut that would most benefit the better off. One told me they would rather the focus had been wooing younger voters by tackling the amount graduates repay in student loans, an old bruise for the Lib Dems.But overall this speech, and this conference, was well received by the Lib Dem faithful.They are a party honing their messaging before the next general election. The strategy is primarily on those 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024. Most of them are held by the Conservatives and Davey's tax cuts are aimed at appealing to those voters.But already the attack from the Tories has been that the Lib Dems are "Labour's lapdog". That attack is in part because Davey has given his most explicit answer this week on not going into a coalition government with the Conservatives after the next general election. He's done the same for Reform UK. But he hasn't ruled out a pact with Labour.So that attack from the Conservatives will come again and again before the next election.But the Lib Dems leave their Brighton conference buoyed, with sights not just on retaining their record 72 seats won at the last election, but on winning some more. And then?"I've got no ceiling on our ambitions," Davey said this week. He has already served in government once, in coalition with David Cameron's Conservatives. His eyes are on another stint in office.

schema.headline: Lib Dems leave conference buoyed by Davey's message

title: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences
description: Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police have said.The charges are an alle
body: Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police have said.The charges are an alleged indecent assault against a teenage girl aged 16 to 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham in 1991 and the alleged sexual assault of an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth in 2004.These charges are in addition to those brought against Westwood, 68, in October 2025 relating to seven women, which include four counts of rape.Westwood has previously denied multiple sex offences, including rape and sexual assault, and pleaded not guilty to earlier charges last December.Westwood is now facing a total of 17 charges involving nine women.Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police Service, said: "The women who have made reports have placed their trust in us, and we remain committed to providing them with all available support."Independent support is also available through Rape Crisis via its 24/7 Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line."Westwood is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court at a future date in relation to the two additional charges, the Met Police said.A trial relating to the original 15 charges is scheduled to begin at Southwark Crown Court on 25 January 2027.Catherine P Baccas, deputy chief crown prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) London, said: "Today the Crown Prosecution Service has authorised two further charges of sexual assault and indecent assault against Tim Westwood."Mr Westwood is already charged with nine counts of indecent assault, two counts of sexual assault and four counts of rape in relation to reported non-recent offences between 1983 and 2016 involving seven women."These new charges, following an investigation by the Metropolitan Police, relate to separate reports of non-recent offences in 1991 and 2004 involving two additional women."Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring these additional charges to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue further criminal proceedings."The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that criminal proceedings are active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial."

schema.headline: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences

title: IMF tells advanced economies to 'bring debt down' as borrowing costs rise
description: The world's advanced economies including the UK and US need to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels following weeks of spiralling government interest
body: The world's advanced economies including the UK and US need to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels following weeks of spiralling government interest costs, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.In an exclusive interview, Kristalina Georgieva said global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost"."[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.The intervention comes as government borrowing costs have surged in response to wars disrupting the supply of oil, which has fuelled inflation.Higher global borrowing costs have hit the UK government in the run-up to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first Budget next month, with speculation building over potential tax and spending policies.The latest figures show borrowing - the difference between tax receipts and government spending - was £18.3bn ($24.4bn) in August, almost a fifth higher than the year before and higher than official forecasts. Meanwhile debt interest for the month was the highest August figure since monthly records began in 1997.Higher borrowing costs have also hit the US, the world's largest economy, which has seen its debt pile surpass $40tn. The amount has doubled within the space of a decade, prompting concerns at home and abroad.On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Georgieva said the IMF's message to advanced economies was that while there were economic factors occurring outside the control of governments, they did have command over domestic policies."There are these two things that must be done: bring debt levels down, put fiscal consolidation as a priority, and make sure that the central banks deliver on their mandate for price stability," she said."It is impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to get the courage to take the steps that are necessary. These are politically tough steps to take, but necessary steps to take."Asked specifically about the UK's higher interest costs compared to other major economies, Georgieva said its position was "not very different" from others. She pointed to "fairly consistent action" on lowering debt and praised planning and housing reforms, adding that advanced economies "don't have the cash" to boost growth and so had to rely on reforms to encourage the private sector to invest.Governments around the world raise money by selling bonds - essentially an IOU - and in return pay interest to the investment funds that buy them.Concerns over inflation eating away at returns has sent the interest rates on bonds - known as yields - higher in recent months. But there are other factors pushing yields up, including increasing competition in the bond market from large tech companies looking to raise huge amounts of money to invest in artificial intelligence (AI) development.On AI, Georgieva referenced recent concerns about loss of safe control over such systems as a potential financial stability problem, alongside debt levels."If we see more incidents when AI takes [on a] life of its own, then we can be faced with a significant financial stability risk," she said.The IMF's managing director repeated the influential body's assessment that the global economy was affected by two forces "pushing in opposite directions" - the energy price shock and investment in AI.She said it was important for the low exports of oil and gas from the Gulf "to resume in a durable manner, for the energy supply shock to finally be in the rearview mirror"."That is a very significant step to normalisation," she said, but acknowledged it was yet to happen.

schema.headline: IMF tells advanced economies to 'bring debt down' as borrowing costs rise

title: England vs Sri Lanka: Will Jacks' career-best 5-22 helps hosts win in Durham
description: First Metro Bank one-day international, Chester-le-StreetEngland 265 (48.1 overs): Brook 67 (69); Colombage 3-44 Sri Lanka 176 (37 overs): Wellalage 4
body: First Metro Bank one-day international, Chester-le-StreetEngland 265 (48.1 overs): Brook 67 (69); Colombage 3-44 Sri Lanka 176 (37 overs): Wellalage 45 (36); Jacks 5-22England won by 89 runsScorecardWill Jacks' all-round efforts helped England grind out an 89-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international at Chester-le-Street to continue their quiet revival in white-ball cricket. Faced with a slow and low pitch, Jacks made 46 not out after 67 from Harry Brook and 44 from Joe Root, meaning England posted 265 despite being bowled out in 48.1 overs.That score appeared only par but a professional bowling performance limited Sri Lanka's scoring and found regular wickets.Jacks took the big wickets of Kusal Mendis and Charith Asalanka and then wrapped up the tail for career-best figures of 5-22. Sri Lanka, much improved in the field but far too timid with the bat, were bowled out for 176.England, who have now won 10 white-ball matches in a row against Sri Lanka this year, can seal a third ODI series win in a row with a game to spare on Thursday at Headingley. The three-match contest concludes on Sunday at The Oval - a match that brings down the curtain on one of the most topsy-turvy summers in recent memory.This was not vintage England. For the first time since 2019 they did not hit a six batting first.Captain Brook and coach Brendon McCullum should not mind that, however. For too long, England have only been able to win when piling up big scores.Yes, they were dismissed for the 12th time since McCullum took charge of the white-ball sides last year and, as so often this summer, the quality of the opposition can be questioned.But Brook was the only batter to fall in a middle order collapse of 4-29 playing an aggressive shot. He sliced a drive to deep cover after batting in a restrained manner, while Sri Lanka's debutant leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage, who found a hint of turn to hit Root's off stump, had Jos Buttler lbw for 31 and bowled Overton with a googly for eight, was impressive.After the collapse, Jacks could have swung hard but batted responsibly to stretch out the innings from 211-7 in the 39th over.He took 18 runs from the 47th over and was primed to cut loose before Asitha Fernando, having dismissed opener Tom Banton for 10 with a bail-trimmer in the powerplay, found reverse swing to bowl Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue. Jacks' importance to England's white-ball sides is growing with every match.They will need bigger scores by the time the World Cup comes around in a year's time but, after beating Sri Lanka at the start of the year and toppling India in July, they are now primed to enter two months of white-ball cricket overseas on the back of another series win.With Adil Rashid out of this series with a hand injury, much of the attention was on Rehan Ahmed, who has a rare chance to press his case as England's leg-spinner.After being carelessly run-out for two, he dropped a caught-and-bowled chance in his first over and conceded 46 runs in seven overs. Those figures were harsh but he will hope for better before the series is out.Instead, it was Jacks who played the lead spinner's role with his off-spin, barely bowling a bad ball.Asalanka and Mendis were pinned attempting sweeps and Dunith Wellalage, who hit two sixes in a 36-ball 45 at number seven, was tempted to sky a catch to mid-on. When Fernando and Dilshan Madushanka followed, Jacks had the best figures by an England spinner since Vic Marks in 1984.England's total was also the lowest they have defended in a full ODI since July 2022 – before their dismal 2023 World Cup or their winless run at last year's Champions Trophy.Gus Atkinson bowled well for 1-25 in seven overs and Jamie Overton 2-21 in five. The seamers all bowled hard lengths and were rewarded.

schema.headline: England vs Sri Lanka: Will Jacks' career-best 5-22 helps hosts win in Durham

title: 'Poison seller' who sold my daughter fatal drugs should rot in hell
description: Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Imogen Nunn died after ingesting a poison she ordered onlineByChristina McSorley and Sean DilleyA Canadian
body: Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Imogen Nunn died after ingesting a poison she ordered onlineByChristina McSorley and Sean DilleyA Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals to people who went on to kill themselves should "rot in hell", the mother of a British woman who took her own life has said.Imogen Nunn, known as Immy, died in January 2023 aged 25 after buying drugs online from Kenneth Law.Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in online suicide forums. But almost 80 deaths in the UK have also been linked to him.However, as part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.Imogen's mother, Louise Nunn, told the BBC she was angry he would not face justice here. "I think we've been let down as families. Our children have been let down," she told the BBC.It comes as the impact statements of UK families will be read in court in Ontario this week.Image caption, "I think we've been let down as families," Louise Nunn told the BBC In May this year, Law pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada as part of a deal with prosecutors, who withdrew more serious charges of murder.Authorities said Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.Speaking at the time, families of British victims said they were angry UK prosecutors had not charged Law over the deaths of 79 Britons, which authorities said were linked to products he supplied.Image source, Peel Regional Police / PA WireImage caption, Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients whom he met in online suicide forums The UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said it had agreed to the Canadian plea bargain on the basis Law's sentence take the British deaths into account.A letter, seen by the BBC, revealed the CPS was concerned Law could challenge his extradition to the UK from Canada, and that including UK victims in the Canadian sentencing process was the "quickest and most effective route" to justice.'You destroyed my whole world'This week, a Canadian court will hear impact statements from UK victims. They will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date. It is the only opportunity for British families to have a voice in the legal process.Speaking to the BBC, however, Nunn said part of her victim impact statement had been redacted by authorities."I think we had a chance to say the words we wanted to say in our impact statement, but now I've been told they've redacted my last paragraph, which felt like our only chance."In it, she said Law destroyed her life. "You have destroyed my whole world. If Immy was here now, I know exactly what she would say to me, but I'm not Immy and I will never forgive you."Immy was profoundly deaf and had a presence on social media where she shared a satirical look at her life."She found social media and I just remember how happy she was," said Nunn. "She tried to put a spin on a sad situation and she tried to take all the negative things in her life and turn it into more positive."It changed her, her confidence came back. Social media built up her confidence and friendships."Responding to the BBC, the CPS said: "Some redactions are being applied to victim impact statements as advised by Canadian counsel, to ensure they are admissible within the Canadian courts."We recognise the profound impact of Kenneth Law's offending and are working to ensure all victims and bereaved families have the opportunity to share their individual experiences through the sentencing process."If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

schema.headline: 'Poison seller' who sold my daughter fatal drugs should rot in hell

title: Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas becomes longest-running number one in US chart history
description: Langley's song was written at a writing retreat in 2024, with assistance from country star Miranda Lambert.Unexpectedly, it started with a discussion
body: Langley's song was written at a writing retreat in 2024, with assistance from country star Miranda Lambert.Unexpectedly, it started with a discussion about a pet kangaroo Lambert had once owned."She told me the story about how she got pulled over [by the police] with a kangaroo in the passenger seat and a dog in the back," Langley explained.The officer was so surprised that she didn't issue a ticket.Langley responded to Lambert, saying the cop must have known she was from Texas, given the chaos unfolding in the car. That prompted the lyric, "She's from Texas, I can tell." Over the next 30 minutes, the writers (who also included Luke Dick and Joybeth Taylor) cooked up a story about a woman in Tennessee, who realises her partner's heart still belongs to Texas... and to another girl.First previewed on stage in February 2025, Langley said she instantly knew it would become the first single from her sophomore album, Dandelion."We loved that song, but I don't think I could ever have imagined what's happening with it right now," the singer told Billboard magazine."Every day I wake up and it's doing something that I didn't even know was a goal I could have had. It's crazy, it's nuts."Its success helped the 27-year-old, who is actually from Alabama, sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May. She won in all seven categories in which she was nominated, including female artist of the year, artist songwriter of the year, and both single and song of the year, for Choosin' Texas.It is now one of only two songs to surpass 20 weeks at number one on the US charts - with the other being Mariah Carey's perennial Christmas smash All I Want for Christmas Is You.But the records for long-running hits have been tumbling ever since streaming became a mainstream phenomenon.For 23 years, Carey's own One Sweet Day, a duet with Boyz II Men, held the title, notching up 16 weeks at number one.Daddy Yankee and Luis Fonsi's Despacito remix, featuring Justin Bieber, tied the record in 2017; then Lil Nas X's Old Town Road surpassed it the following year, eventually spending 19 weeks at the top.All I Want for Christmas Is You eventually overtook that, thanks to its habit of returning to the charts every December.But critics say that streaming services are increasingly encouraging listeners to play the same playlists of familiar songs over and over again, creating a bottleneck that makes it harder for new music to break through.In 2022, a report by the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, external found that more than 60% of streams were of music recorded by only the top 0.4% of artists.

schema.headline: Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas becomes longest-running number one in US chart history

title: 'Peeing a jellyfish': Children's ketamine injuries revealed
description: The drug is a general anaesthetic so it reduces or blunts sensations in the body. Users say it can make them feel dream-like and detached, chilled and
body: The drug is a general anaesthetic so it reduces or blunts sensations in the body. Users say it can make them feel dream-like and detached, chilled and relaxed. But it can also cause extreme harm. Prof Rachel Isba who runs the clinic told the BBC some of the children she has seen had started wetting the bed or having to go to the toilet more often and in a hurry. "Sometimes they don't always make it. They might have accidents...and a lot of them report pain in their bladder."They describe this feeling of weeing over broken glass. It's very painful."She says, unfortunately, some of them will use the ketamine to treat the pain."Ketamine is a very good pain reliever. It's an anaesthetic, and so they get into a vicious cycle or 'K loop', which makes their bladder worse," says Isba.She says ketamine is very cheap, "pocket-money level"."And you only need a small amount to feel an effect."She says some children find it hard to quit if their mates are still doing it. "There's use going on at school. That's really difficult. And, unfortunately for many of these children they are not able to attend education for various reasons."Some had pre-existing conditions like ADHD, while others had been in and out of the care system.Ketamine abuse in children and young people is on the rise in the UK.The Alder Hey doctors, external saw one young patient in 2023, nine in 2024, and then "a rapid escalation" in 2025, which led them to open the bespoke clinic in May.They get about one referral every week from GPs or emergency departments in Cheshire, Merseyside and other nearby regions. Of the first 60 they saw, 43 were girls. Despite its name, "ketamine bladder" can affect the entire urinary tract, including the kidneys and ureters.Symptoms include an urgent and frequent need to urinate. This can be very painful and the pee can be blood-stained. Although stopping using ketamine can help, sometimes the damage can be so serious that the bladder needs surgical repair or even removal.Some users experience abdominal pain and spasms, or "K cramps" too.There are reports that heavy users are getting liver damage, but it is difficult to separate harms from other things people may also be taking, including other street drugs and alcohol. Isba says cannabis and alcohol are still more popular, but ketamine is "probably up into third place". Children at the clinic often say they have also tried other drugs, drank alcohol, and vaped.About three out of every 10 people who frequently use ketamine get bladder issues, says the British Association of Urological Surgeons, external.Sometimes it is reversible, if the drug use stops. Given the risks, there have been calls to reclassify it as a Class A drug - like cocaine and heroin - but the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs has recommended to government that ketamine should remain a Class B controlled substance, like amphetamines and cannabis.Isba says children are disadvantaged when it comes to accessing services."There are definitely some children out there who are under the age of 16 who if they were 18 would be offered an inpatient detox stay. But because we don't have those facilities in the UK, they are not able to access that and that feels unfair. Particularly for the ones who are ready to stop."

schema.headline: 'Peeing a jellyfish': Children's ketamine injuries revealed

title: Earl Spencer should pull Diana book, Piers Morgan says
description: Piers Morgan has called for Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana to be pulled from the shelves over a factual error. Earl Spencer, Princess Diana'
body: Piers Morgan has called for Earl Spencer's book about Princess Diana to be pulled from the shelves over a factual error. Earl Spencer, Princess Diana's brother, apologised to Morgan for incorrectly describing him in the memoir as the editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group published "highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym" in 1993.Speaking to the BBC, Morgan said he accepted the apology but that his lawyers would be "laying out that we want the offending pages to be removed from this book. And if that means they pulp the first edition, so be it".The BBC understands Penguin, the publishers of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, will be amending this one point in future editions of the book.The photographs of Princess Diana mentioned in relation to Morgan in Earl Spencer's book were published by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993.At the time, Morgan was working at The Sun and did not join the Mirror as its editor until 1995.Earl Spencer admitted "his assumption was incorrect" and "apologises to Mr Morgan for this error", a statement said.On his YouTube show, Piers Morgan Uncensored, Morgan read out a section of the book - which was published on 22 September - in which Earl Spencer wrote: "They realised they were unable to be rude to the brother of the much-mourned princess…"The only one who sounded surly, as opposed to merely confused or embarrassed, was Piers Morgan of the Mirror, who snarled with annoyance before he hung up."I assumed Morgan must be feeling particular guilt because, four years earlier, he and his Sunday Mirror counterpart had published photographs taken with hidden cameras by a gym owner. They were of Diana working out in a leotard."This was such an intolerable invasion of her privacy that Diana instructed lawyers to sue the Mirror Group and to block further use of the images."The settlement Princess Diana's lawyers came to in 1995 was never publicly disclosed, but it was believed that Mirror Group Newspapers (MGN) paid Princess Diana's legal costs of about £1m and about £200,000 to charities of her choice.A spokesperson for Princess Diana's brother said in a statement: "Earl Spencer's account of his conversation with Piers Morgan is accurate. Mr Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister's funeral."The statement admitted the factual error, and said that "as an historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologises to Mr Morgan for this error".Speaking to the BBC, Morgan said: "He's a historian. He should want it removed from the shelves. Why, if you're doing this for historical record, would you want such a completely untrue series of claims over several pages about a public figure to still be in that book?"Now you've admitted it's untrue and apologised. He should pull the book."In a post on social media on Tuesday, Morgan said he was "pursuing legal action against him and his publisher Penguin to have the lies removed, and damages paid to the King's Trust".Swan Song, which contains a string of allegations including that King Charles said "we'll forget her soon enough" in the days after her death, has led to a war of words between the Earl and Buckingham Palace.The book claims the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Princess Diana's funeral procession.In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".Separately on Tuesday, The Telegraph reported that Prince Harry is in talks to make a documentary about his mother, Diana.Earl Spencer's book also alludes to a "nephew" who wanted him to be in a documentary about Diana, which will further raise speculation about Harry's plans for the 30th anniversary of his mother's death next year.BBC News understands Prince Harry has discussed a number of possible projects to mark the anniversary and is still considering the most meaningful way to honour her legacy.

schema.headline: Earl Spencer should pull Diana book, Piers Morgan says

title: Tennis: British player Tara Moore's latest legal bid over doping ban dismissed by US court
description: In April 2022, Moore tested positive for nandrolone and boldenone at a WTA 250 event in Bogota, with an independent tribunal ruling in December 2023 t
body: In April 2022, Moore tested positive for nandrolone and boldenone at a WTA 250 event in Bogota, with an independent tribunal ruling in December 2023 that contaminated meat was the source.Moore, who was Britain's leading women's doubles player at the time of the failed test, was found to bear "no fault or negligence", but the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) appealed against the decision.Last year, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) ruled in favour of the ITIA and Moore was banned until 2028.Moore then initiated proceedings with the American Arbitration Association, in which she claimed the WTA's "failure to warn against eating meat in Colombia was a direct cause of her positive test result and the harm that followed".The arbitrator supported the ruling made by Cas and dismissed the case against the WTA. In response, Moore filed a motion against the decision at the United States District Court in New York.Moore, who was ranked a career-high 77th in the world in 2022, claimed she was denied a fair hearing by the arbitrator.The motion detailed how Moore was seeking "no less than $20m in compensatory damages" after claiming the WTA "stayed silent in the face of a known and specific danger and then shifted the blame for its own negligence" to the player.On Friday, United States district judge Andrew Carter found Moore's challenge was "not justified" on a legal basis.The WTA and ITIA have been approached for comment.

schema.headline: Tennis: British player Tara Moore's latest legal bid over doping ban dismissed by US court

title: Kylian Mbappe reveals he was 'close' to joining Liverpool in 2016
description: Kylian Mbappe has revealed how "close" he came to joining Liverpool in 2016, saying he went against the advice of his mother who "fell in love" with A
body: Kylian Mbappe has revealed how "close" he came to joining Liverpool in 2016, saying he went against the advice of his mother who "fell in love" with Anfield.The France and Real Madrid striker said the Reds tried to sign him at 18, while he was playing for Monaco in Ligue 1.Former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp said the club laid on a private jet and food for Mbappe and his family in an attempt to sign him, before he eventually joined Paris St-Germain.Speaking to the Athletic, Mbappe said his mum was a "big fan" of Klopp and wanted her son to move to Merseyside."I was close to [joining] Liverpool. The favourite destination for my mum was Liverpool. She wanted me to go there," he said."I didn't listen because I wanted to play in my city, Paris. I didn't want to leave my country before I was someone. "But yes, my mum was always saying, 'Liverpool - you're going to be there, playing at Anfield, it's going to be insane for you'."Mbappe, now 27, said his mother went out to Liverpool for the "first step" of the negotiation."She went to the city, the stadium, she met the people. She was like, 'it's a wonderful club, everybody's so kind, it's a family club, a big club', said Mbappe."She went to Anfield and fell in love with it. She watched a few games alone, to feel the atmosphere, because she wanted to imagine me in this stadium."Klopp, who spoke about the possible move on Magenta TV as a pundit at the 2026 World Cup, explained how a flight was taken from Blackpool to Nice in France, where "the entire Mbappe family boarded a private jet with five rooms or something"."We really went all out. Then we flew around in a circle, talked with the family, ate good food," Klopp said.He said they had not wanted to be seen having talks - but the meeting proved fruitless."We flew in a circle. It was fantastic. And then he went to Paris," Klopp added."It's a funny story," said Mbappe."But in the end, I took the decision to go to PSG because for me, born and raised in Paris, there was no better feeling than to show I could be a star in my hometown."Mbappe later joined PSG on loan, in a deal including an option for the move to become permanent for 180m euros (£165.7m). He went on to spend seven years in Paris, becoming the club's record scorer before leaving for Real Madrid in 2024.

schema.headline: Kylian Mbappe reveals he was 'close' to joining Liverpool in 2016

title: Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal
description: US President Donald Trump has said Andy Burnham is a man he can do business with, after the two leaders met in person for the first time.Trump said UK
body: US President Donald Trump has said Andy Burnham is a man he can do business with, after the two leaders met in person for the first time.Trump said UK-US relations are "more up now" that Burnham is in power, following their meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.Speaking to reporters, Burnham said he had "established a good connection" with Trump and they had "taken that further today" following discussions on issues such as trade and immigration.But the US president made clear his opposition to the UK's "terrible" deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back a joint UK-US military base on the archipelago's largest island, Diego Garcia.Burnham, asked by broadcasters if the deal is "dead", later said the UK will "work hard" to find a resolution between the different sides and he is "confident we can find it working with our US partners".Trump and Burnham met on Tuesday as they attended the United Nations for the annual gathering of world leaders.Following bilateral talks, Burnham sat alongside Trump and used his opening remarks to say: "You and I have established a good connection in our early discussions and we've taken that further today."The two men then faced questions shouted from the assembled press pack.Asked by the BBC if Burnham was a man he could do business with, Trump said: "Yeah I do, I think he's a natural businessperson, we've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting we've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone."Yeah, I think so, he gets it, he understands what he has to do."Burnham later said he had explained to Trump that Britain has been in "too much turbulence" in recent times but it is time to "turn the story" about the country into a positive one.The US president added that the UK is a country with "great patriotism", and he thinks it is "waiting for good leadership, waiting for success".Relations between Sir Keir and Trump also began well before becoming increasingly strained earlier this year when the then-prime minister refused to permit the use of UK bases for the initial US-Israel strikes on Iran.Trump reiterated his criticism of the Chagos Islands deal and stressed how a joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia is "strategically very important", particularly in relation to US operations in Iran.The agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back the military base - but in April the deal was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.Speaking on Tuesday, Trump said: "I think the prime minister is going to be looking at [the deal]."Burnham replied: "Yep."He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution".Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well."What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who has long been a critic of the deal, posted on X: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God."One of the areas Burnham has been keen to focus on during his trip to the UN is artificial intelligence (AI).The prime minister met business leaders, including Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook, on Tuesday. He told them he wants a "single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks".Burnham's approach could cause friction with Trump, with the president using his address to the UN General Assembly to say that the US "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI.Trump dubbed AI as "super intelligence" and said the US will "encourage it, not rein it in".Burnham later met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, with the PM apologising for arriving around 10 minutes late due to his bilateral with Trump running over.Von der Leyen reassured the PM, saying: "These things are understandable."

schema.headline: Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal

title: 'I tossed books across the room': Booker Prize judges reveal 'tussle' over shortlist
description: Past Booker Prize winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart have been shortlisted for the prestigious literary award again, after a selection process th
body: Past Booker Prize winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart have been shortlisted for the prestigious literary award again, after a selection process that the judges described as "a tussle".Jamaican writer James is nominated this year for his latest novel The Disappearers; while Scottish author Stuart is shortlisted for John of John.This year's other contenders are award-winning US novelist Elizabeth Strout, and British authors M John Harrison, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry.But seven books that appeared on the longlist in July have been jettisoned, and Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the judging panel, said agreeing on the final six "has been, to put it mildly, hard work".Scroll down to find out more about this year's nominees.James previously won the Booker Prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, while Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain.Praising this year's entries, Dame Mary added: "English language fiction now is full of talent – talent old and talent new. "It's full of wit, seriousness, pleasure, challenge, discomfort and real brilliance, and I think we should be rewarding our novelists a lot more than we do."The other judges included former Booker Prize-shortlisted US novelist Patricia Lockwood, who said she discovered she was "bossier than I believed myself to be" when making the case for or against particular books in the judges' meetings."I was sort of standing up a lot and tossing books across the room and being really active. I was like, 'Wow, yeah, I didn't know I had it in me'."Another judge, poet Raymond Antrobus, told reporters: "All of us individually had a different idea for a shortlist and then it was a tussle."Lockwood jokingly added: "A tussle, yeah. We wrestled like pigs in the mud!"Antrobus said the final choices are connected because they are books that "as well as having heart, also took risk"."These books, we truly believe, cannot be replicated by artificial intelligence. These are very human books for the way they talk about and navigate a lived experience."The judging line-up was completed by journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu and Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, who said being on the selection panel was "a bit like being in a band".He said: "The way a band makes an appealing noise is by everybody combining, in a way, and if you don't like that then you have to go solo."You get something that you couldn't get [alone] and no-one's in control of it and you make a good noise together. So I hope that's what this shortlist is, a nice noise."Cocker read some of the entries while on tour, and said he joined one judges' meeting online while wearing a dressing gown in a hotel room in Australia at 02:00 local time."When you're on tour, it's quite dull when you're travelling so it was quite good to have something to read," he said."I became known for being in those meetings wearing a towelling robe."The End of Everything by M John HarrisonAn unexplained catastrophe, and the arrival of mysterious alien beings, have turned British society upside down - and a man and his elderly aunt muddle through on the Kent coast. It's the author's first Booker nomination, and he'd be the oldest ever winner at 81.The judges said: "The End of Everything can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism. The landscape may be bleak, the catastrophe may be immersive, yet there still were moments we found ourselves laughing aloud."The Disappearers by Marlon JamesThis epic, visceral story revolves around a violent attack on eight gay men who had gathered to rehearse a queer play in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988, and its aftermath. The New York Times called it "a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century thus far".The judges said: "A Jamaican epic from one of the most impactful Caribbean novelists today; readers will love the shifting register of the dialogue and poetic phrasings, often pierced through with sharp, double-edged humour."Black Bag by Luke KennardAn out-of work actor gets a new role - being locked in a black bag during psychology lectures for an entire term as a professor's experiment. The story unfolds into a humorous and poignant satire that makes sharp observations about the state of modern masculinity and creative life.The judges said: "In a wonderfully quirky campus novel, Kennard combines an absurd experiment with a moving story about human frailty, passion, confusion and identity. There's something for everyone here."May We Feed the King by Rebecca PerryA modern-day museum curator is commissioned to recreate a past scene in a historic palace, and becomes immersed in the world of the young, reluctant king whose life she uncovers. It is the debut novel by Perry, who is also a poet and a former competitive trampolinist.The judges said: "An affecting and lush jewel of a novel that moves between our present-day world to a medieval court and unsettles the idea that there's ever one universal historical truth."The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth StroutStrout, a former Pulitzer Prize winner and double Booker nominee, tells the story of a high school history teacher in his 50s who feels adrift in modern America. When a secret emerges, he must face big questions about his relationships and life choices.The judges said: "A novel that engages with the deeply divisive politics of present-day America, without itself becoming divisive. This is the kind of book we need now: a calm antidote to contemporary events."John of John by Douglas StuartThe third novel by Stuart is about a fashion student who is drawn back to his home in a small, religious community in the Outer Hebrides in the mid-1990s. He and his father both nurse secrets. And both are called John.The judges said: "A rich and moving novel about a father and son who live on a remote Scottish island in the 1990s, where small-town secrets and buried shame reverberate to surprising, devastating and even joyous effect."The winner will receive £50,000 and will be announced in London on 9 November. The ceremony will be broadcast live on a special edition of BBC Radio 4's Front Row.Longlisted books that did not make the final cut included Emma Cline's Switzy, which had been seen by some as a frontrunner for the prize."Believe me, this is a nailed-on Booker winner," critic Giles Coren wrote in the Times, external this weekend."If this one doesn't win, I'll eat Mary Beard."Dame Mary responded on Tuesday: "I know Giles Coren said he wants to eat me if Switzy isn't on the shortlist."Well, I'm going to get the cooker prepared and ask him how he wants me done."

schema.headline: 'I tossed books across the room': Booker Prize judges reveal 'tussle' over shortlist

title: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
description: The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffir
body: The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it. Before a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations".Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win".The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory.Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth.His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral". The deal amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US.The new pact says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east.Narsarsuaq is a former civilian airport and World War Two base. It has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were recently surveying, the US North Command confirmed to the BBC.The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit.The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties, This means the US security arrangements are not unfettered and Greenland and Denmark's approval is still needed.Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there. It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland".Although the militaries of non-Nato countries are now explicitly barred from the island, it was highly unlikely that non-allied troops would have been allowed access in the first place.Critically, no territory is ceded to the US, and it recognises both Denmark's  "sovereignty and territorial integrity" and Greenland's right to self-determination.On one hand, that's a significant climb down from Trump's earlier calls to acquire the Arctic island.But it does deliver a strengthened US military presence and expand on the previous agreement. Therefore to some American eyes, that will be perceived as a historic win.The new deal must still be approved by both Denmark's and Greenland's parliaments.Despite months of crisis, the mood at Tuesday's signing ceremony appeared strikingly upbeat and friendly."We going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship," Trump said."This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland it's going to be incredible."Meanwhile, Frederiksen described the signing of the deal as a "milestone in our long-standing co-operation". "Seventy-five years ago we entered into an agreement about the defence of Greenland. Today, we're signing an even bigger and better agreement - a deal that can last forever."The Danish prime minister stressed that the agreement "respects sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland's right to self-determination".Jens-Frederik Nielsen said that "for Greenland, it is not only an agreement about us, it is [an] agreement with us."It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country."Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security," he said, adding that the Nato had a key role to play in the North Atlantic in a changing security situation.The agreement also confirmed Greenland would remain in Nato if it were to gain independence from Denmark.The 1951 agreement already allowed the US to send as many troops as it wanted to Greenland. Washington already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base.Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.He argued the Arctic island was an essential piece of his plan to build a futuristic "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US against missile attacks. However the deal only mentions the project once, and contains no concrete proposal.A Nato spokesperson said shortly afterwards that the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".In Denmark, the deal is being hailed as a triumph of diplomacy, and several political parties in Denmark have already said they would back it.For Greenland, a country of 56,000 people, there was good reason for a big sigh of relief. Its leader sat side-by-side with the world's most powerful man, and got a deal that should now bring an end to months of crisis.

schema.headline: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark

title: Henry Pollock: Eddie Hearn says back row 'left money on the table' with Northampton deal
description: Henry Pollock turned down rival offers worth hundreds of thousands of pounds more than his extension to stay at boyhood club Northampton, says Eddie H
body: Henry Pollock turned down rival offers worth hundreds of thousands of pounds more than his extension to stay at boyhood club Northampton, says Eddie Hearn.Hearn, whose Matchroom promotional empire is centred on boxing, darts and snooker, has been working as Pollock's adviser since March.Pollock, 21, has agreed a new deal with Saints that extends his terms to summer 2028 and is worth more than £400,000 a year."There were a couple of domestic offers – a couple of Prem offers - and international offers as well," said Hearn of Pollock's options during his renegotiation."We had a very, very straight conversation. I said to him, 'be honest, do you want to go?' And he went, 'no, I really don't want to go'. And that was it."He knew the numbers, but ultimately he just wanted to stay at the club."He left a lot of money on the table to stay with Northampton. But it wasn't even a tough decision for him."Hearn says that some of Pollock's suitors were offering "well in excess of seven figures".The £1m mark was where Hearn valued Pollock's annual salary prospects in an interview with the Daily Telegraph interview in August., externalHearn acknowledges that his client's new deal "didn't quite get to the number" that was targeted.The headline basic figure Pollock has accepted does not account for a signing bonus and various payments he receives for off-pitch work.And Hearn says that Pollock's endorsement deals have carried him comfortably over £1m in total annual earnings."Everybody from major financial institutions to household brands to performance brands to nutritional brands to wellness brands… I mean, there isn't really a sector that hasn't hasn't approached us about Henry Pollock," said Hearn.Pollock is keen to explore the possibility of representing Great Britain in rugby sevens at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.GB's qualification is far from certain after the programme went part-time and the team slipped from the top tier of the international circuit.The back row's new deal does not include the sort of dedicated time to train up for sevens that France captain Antoine Dupont took before Paris 2024, but the prospect has been raised with Saints."Our principal obligation is to perform for Northampton and to help them win championships," said Hearn."Part of the arrangement allows him to look at those kind of opportunities, but only with a sensible conversation with the club."Pollock's ability to maximise his on-pitch earnings in England is restricted by a £6.4m salary cap for Prem clubs.Each team is allowed one player whose salary is exempt from the calculations; however, players who move between top-tier teams can only qualify for such marquee status after two years with their new side.Hearn would scrap the cap entirely."Let the players earn," he said. "All they hear about is salary caps or one star player per team - marquee names or whatever you want to call it. You don't want that."You want to say to a young player, 'hey, come to rugby, you can be a superstar and you can earn a fortune'."You could have lost Pollock and it would have been a disaster for English rugby."The salary cap is designed to make the Prem sustainable and competitive, with similar systems in place in most major American sports.Players such as Pollock can supplement club earnings with a central England contract, worth about £150,000 a year, or one-off Test match fees.Still, some England players, such as Jack Willis, Kyle Sinckler and Sam Simmonds, have left for France's Top 14 where a salary cap of 11m euros (£9.4m) offers scope for greater earnings.Hearn's current stable of rugby stars is only two strong. Bath and Scotland fly-half Finn Russell is similarly represented by Matchroom in off-pitch matters and advised by Hearn.However, Hearn has ambitions to become more deeply involved in the staging and promotion of the game. He is set to meet with Prem Rugby chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor in Monaco in the coming weeks to discuss ideas."We haven't really touched the surface in terms of what we could do in the sport," said Hearn."All I've done is done a few deals with Henry, he's come to a couple of fights and I've done a couple of Zoom calls [with journalists]."That just shows you the buzz that can be created with a little bit of hype and perception."But hype and perception are nothing without substance. The sport and the brand is the substance and it's significant in rugby."Look at what Matchroom has done elsewhere. Boxing was dead, darts was non-existent, snooker was stuck in the air. We don't fail. Our track record is second to none."If we went into rugby, it would be a stroll in the park for me. It's a huge global sport steeped in history with fantastic values and tradition that just needs to be just turbo-charged."

schema.headline: Henry Pollock: Eddie Hearn says back row 'left money on the table' with Northampton deal
